name: Make paper airplanes optimized for distance
blurb: Distance planes are an engineering problem: weight forward, wings straight, folds sharp. Understanding why they fly makes the difference between 5 metres and 25.
gear: A4 or letter paper, standard weight
A long corridor or a calm outdoor space
steps: Learn the aerodynamics: the centre of gravity must be forward of the centre of lift, or the plane stalls and tumbles.
Fold a proven distance design — a dart variant or the Suzanne-style world record design — with absolutely symmetrical folds.
Crease hard. Sharp creases hold the aerofoil shape; soft ones let it deform in flight.
Add dihedral: a slight upward V to the wings, which gives roll stability.
Learn the throw: hard, at about 40 degrees for distance, released cleanly without twisting the wrist.
Test and trim — bend the trailing edges up slightly if it dives, down if it stalls — and measure every flight.
tips: Asymmetry is the number one cause of a plane that veers. Fold on a hard surface and check both sides match.
A plane that climbs steeply then stalls is nose-light. Add a fold or a small paperclip at the nose.
proof: A plane you folded flies over 20 metres, straight, three throws in a row.
